title: Database Security, Parameters and Least Privilege
description: Build an authorization model for database operations, distinguish parameter binding from ownership checks, and test least privilege, privacy and audit boundaries.

references.title: OWASP SQL Injection Prevention Cheat Sheet

questions.question_text: What does authentication establish?
questions.explanation: Authorization must still decide what the established identity may do.

questions.question_text: Can an injection-safe query still expose another learner’s data?
options: Yes, if authorization scoping is missing
Only if a column is numeric
questions.explanation: Separating data from SQL syntax does not establish resource ownership.

questions.question_text: What is the primary purpose of binding query values?
options: Let users choose any SQL structure
Keep supplied values in data positions
questions.explanation: A prepared template distinguishes executable structure from supplied values.

questions.question_text: Which value should supply the ownership predicate?
options: Any owner identifier supplied by the browser
The first row in the table
The identity established at a trusted boundary
questions.explanation: An untrusted owner argument does not prove the caller is that owner.

questions.question_text: Can a normal value placeholder select an arbitrary column name?
options: No, identifiers need a trusted structural choice
Only if the name includes spaces
questions.explanation: Identifiers and value literals occupy different roles in a statement.

questions.question_text: How should a public sort choice be handled?
options: Map approved choices to fixed trusted expressions
Strip one quote and trust everything else
questions.explanation: An allow-list bounds the structural variation the operation permits.

questions.question_text: Is a stored procedure automatically safe from injection?
options: Only when it returns two rows
No, dynamic SQL can still concatenate untrusted input
Only when it has a short name
questions.explanation: The actual dynamic execution boundary must preserve the data/code separation.

questions.question_text: What is least privilege?
options: One administrator account for all clients
All privileges until a failure occurs
Only the capabilities required for a defined responsibility
questions.explanation: Narrow capabilities reduce exposure when a component is misused or compromised.

questions.question_text: Does a role’s existence prove it is active in a session?
options: Only if it was created yesterday
questions.explanation: Effective privileges depend on account paths and activation state.

questions.question_text: What must a disabled client button be complemented by?
options: Trusted enforcement of the requested operation
questions.explanation: Callers can bypass the interface and issue direct requests.

questions.question_text: An authorized learner requests another learner’s loan. What should the scoped lookup do?
options: Fetch it with an unscoped fallback
Return no permitted match without broadening the query
questions.explanation: Failure to match the authorization scope is a denial, not a reason to bypass that scope.

questions.question_text: Why keep reporting and migration authority separate?
options: Schema changes are ordinary read operations
questions.explanation: The running report need not hold privileges required only for reviewed schema work.

questions.question_text: Why is a definer-context routine a sensitive boundary?
options: It proves every input is authorized
It can execute with privileges different from the caller’s
questions.explanation: Its elevated capabilities must be exposed only through carefully constrained operations.

questions.question_text: What should a loan summary generally return?
options: Only fields needed for the approved purpose
questions.explanation: Data minimization limits unnecessary disclosure through otherwise permitted operations.

questions.question_text: Does stored-data encryption prevent an authorized SQL session from reading permitted rows?
questions.explanation: Encryption and SQL authorization address different access paths.

questions.question_text: Why include exports in the access model?
options: They can expose protected data in bulk
They automatically inherit every desired rule
questions.explanation: A protected detail path does not compensate for an unrestricted listing or export.

questions.question_text: Which audit content should usually be avoided?
options: Raw credentials and unnecessary personal payloads
questions.explanation: Logs can become a second sensitive data store if they capture excess values.

questions.question_text: Does a trigger alone prove a complete tamper-resistant audit system?
options: Only if the table has ten columns
questions.explanation: Coverage, alternate paths, privilege boundaries and integrity controls require separate evidence.

questions.question_text: What should a denied-access test establish?
options: An administrator can read all rows
The forbidden effect did not occur under the actual enforcing identity
A mock always returns an empty array
questions.explanation: Authorization evidence belongs at the trusted enforcement boundary.

questions.question_text: How should SQL punctuation in a legitimate name be treated?
options: As a reason to remove the person’s name
questions.explanation: Correct binding preserves legitimate text without converting it into query structure.

coding_not_applicable: Security requires permitted and denied operations under actual trusted identities and prepared-statement interfaces. Notes contain worked lookup and privilege-matrix labs; a result-only single-query judge cannot establish injection resistance or authorization.

notes:
## Protect a specific resource and action

Database security controls who can perform an action on which data, under what conditions, and with what evidence afterward. Authentication establishes an identity; authorization decides whether that identity may read or change the requested resource. Encryption, injection prevention, auditing and recovery address additional threats. None of these controls automatically replaces the others. A query can be injection-safe and still disclose another person's records if its authorization predicate is missing.

Imagine an equipment service where learners see their own loans and a desk operator records returns. The important questions are concrete: who may view a loan, who may close it, which identity supplies the ownership condition, and what happens when a request names a loan belonging to someone else? Begin with these operations rather than granting broad table access and hoping the interface hides dangerous buttons.

## Keep values separate from SQL structure

An injection vulnerability appears when untrusted input becomes executable SQL structure. Binding values through a correctly used prepared-statement interface keeps those values in data positions. It does not mean suspicious-looking input must be stripped of apostrophes. A learner named O'Connor should remain representable without turning the name into a fragment of a query. Keep the SQL template and its supplied values separate throughout the trusted data-access path.

The following SQL-level example demonstrates binding a value in MySQL on a disposable fixture. It is an illustration of value binding, not a complete application authentication system. The caller must already have an authorized learner identity and bind that trusted identity rather than simply trusting an owner identifier supplied in a browser request.

```sql
PREPARE loan_lookup FROM
  'SELECT loan_id,asset_id,due_date FROM loan_security_lab
   WHERE learner_id=? AND loan_id=?';
SET @authorized_learner=41;
SET @requested_loan=700;
EXECUTE loan_lookup USING @authorized_learner,@requested_loan;
DEALLOCATE PREPARE loan_lookup;
```

Suppose the fixture contains loan seven hundred for learner forty-one and loan seven hundred one for learner forty-two. The first binding may return the first loan. Binding the second loan identifier while retaining authorized learner forty-one should return no matching row. The empty result is intentional denial through the scoped lookup; it must not trigger an unscoped fallback query that retrieves the loan anyway.

## Allow-list identifiers instead of pretending to bind them

A value placeholder ordinarily cannot choose an arbitrary table name, column name or ASC versus DESC keyword. Those are parts of SQL structure. If a request allows sorting, map a small external choice such as due-date to a fixed trusted expression. Reject unsupported choices or select a documented default. The map should contain application-owned SQL fragments, not strings copied from the request after a superficial character replacement.

Escaping alone is a fragile primary defense because its meaning depends on the driver, character encoding, SQL mode and context. A technique intended for a string literal does not safely authorize an identifier or expression. Likewise, a stored procedure is not automatically injection-safe if it builds dynamic SQL by concatenating its parameters. Trace the final execution boundary, including dynamic statements hidden inside routines.

## Separate application accounts from administration

Least privilege means granting only the capabilities an identity needs for its defined work. A reporting account can need selected read access without needing schema changes or account administration. A migration operator can need privileges that the running application does not. Using one administrator account everywhere broadens the impact of an application defect and makes attribution harder because unrelated operations share the same authority.

MySQL roles collect privileges, while accounts and activation rules determine which privileges are effective. A role existing in the catalog does not prove that every intended session has activated it or that an unintended account lacks another privilege path. Test the actual effective identity and active roles in a disposable authorization lab. Changing real grants requires the system's reviewed administrative workflow, not copying commands from an educational article into production.

| Identity | Example responsibility | Capability to keep separate |
|---|---|---|
| Learner-facing application | Authorized loan lookups and requests | Account administration and schema ownership |
| Desk workflow | Authorized return operation | Unrestricted export of unrelated personal data |
| Reporting workflow | Approved summarized measures | Mutation of operational records |
| Migration operator | Reviewed schema evolution | Routine use as the public application identity |

## Design narrow trusted operations

A narrowly scoped routine or service operation can enforce several conditions together: the actor is authorized, the loan exists in that actor's permitted scope, and the requested state transition is valid. The trusted operation should reject repeated or conflicting actions according to an explicit rule. A client-side disabled button is useful feedback but is not enforcement because a caller can issue a direct request without using the page.

Definer and invoker execution contexts require particular care. A definer-context routine can exercise privileges different from the caller's and therefore becomes a trusted boundary. It must not expose arbitrary SQL execution or trust unchecked ownership arguments. An invoker-context operation still needs the appropriate underlying privileges and row-scoping logic. Neither label, by itself, proves that cross-user access is denied.

## Minimize exposed data and protect recovery copies

Return only columns needed for the operation. A desk report can often show a loan identifier and status without including unrelated contact information. Restrict pagination, exports and broad search paths according to the same authorization model as individual lookups. Otherwise a carefully protected detail endpoint can coexist with an unrestricted listing that exposes the same records in bulk.

Protect transport and stored recovery artifacts using the organization's supported controls. Database encryption does not prevent an authorized SQL session from reading data that its privileges permit. Backups, exports, temporary files and binary logs can contain sensitive contents outside the normal application interface. Their storage location, access rules and retention deserve explicit decisions. Keep credentials in approved secret references and avoid printing values in diagnostics or teaching reports.

## Audit useful events without creating another leak

An audit record should explain a meaningful action: actor reference, operation, target reference, time and outcome. Include a correlation identifier that connects the request with trusted server processing. Avoid recording raw passwords, full bound payloads or unnecessary personal data. A log that captures every query argument may become a second, less protected copy of the very information the application is trying to safeguard.

Audit availability and integrity matter too. Decide who can read the records, who can modify them, how retention works and what happens if the logging path fails. A trigger alone does not establish a complete tamper-resistant audit system: privileged users, alternate paths and external activity need separate consideration. Distinguish evidence of an attempted denied request from evidence that a protected mutation actually occurred.

## Define failure behavior at the boundary

Database errors should become useful application outcomes without revealing internal connection strings or private provider diagnostics. A caller may need to know that a request was rejected, while the operator needs a safe correlation identifier for investigation. Preserve the distinction between an unavailable database, an unauthorized resource and an invalid state transition in the trusted implementation, even when a public response deliberately limits detail. Do not convert every failure into a successful empty result and then assume the security test passed; verify the protected state as well as the response.

## Work through permitted and denied access exercises

First exercise: build a disposable fixture containing the two learners' loans. Execute the scoped prepared lookup for the correct owner, the wrong owner and a nonexistent identifier. The solution returns the permitted loan only in the first case and does not issue a broader fallback for either denial. Add an input containing SQL punctuation as a bound text value in a separate name lookup. Its punctuation remains data; it must not alter the query's structure or broaden the result.

Second exercise: create a permission matrix for reporting, desk and migration identities in an isolated authorization environment. Test the approved operation and a forbidden operation under each effective identity. The solution records actual allowed and denied outcomes, including active-role state, without weakening grants to make a test pass. A mock client response or a single SELECT as an administrator does not prove the application's authorization boundary.

Review [view security](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/view-security) for another place where execution context and exposed columns matter, and [business constraints](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/business-constraints) for valid state transitions. The goal is a small, reviewable set of trusted capabilities whose success, denial and failure behavior can all be demonstrated. Injection prevention, least privilege, privacy and auditing work together only when their separate responsibilities remain explicit.
